structured.lead: Jeremy Collier's A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage attacked among others
structured.options_hint: John Bunyan Thomas Rhymer William Congre

items.explanation: In his polemical tract A Short View of the Immorality, and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698), Jeremy Collier fiercely attacked Restoration comedy playwrights, most notably William Congreve, John Vanbrugh, John Dryden, and William Wycherley.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Charles Darwin

of the Great Exhibition, was
designed by

structured.lead: The Crystal Palace, a key exhibit of the Great Exhibition, was designed by
structured.options_hint: Charles Darwin Edward Moxon Joseph Paxto

items.explanation: Sir Joseph Paxton, an English gardener and architect, designed the monumental cast-iron and plate-glass Crystal Palace erected in London's Hyde Park to house the Great Exhibition of 1851.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Tom Stoppard
items.stem:
Influence of the Indian Philosophy
is seen in the writings of

structured.lead: Influence of the Indian Philosophy is seen in the writings of
structured.options_hint: Shaw Noel Coward Tom Stoppard Eliot

items.explanation: T. S. Eliot studied Sanskrit, Pali, and Indian philosophy at Harvard University, deeply incorporating teachings from the Upanishads ('Datta. Dayadhvam. Damyata.'), the Bhagavad Gita, and Buddhist texts into The Waste Land (1922) and Four Quartets (1943).

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism

structured.lead: In which of his voyages, Gulliver discovered mountain-like beings ?
structured.options_hint: The land of the Lilliputians The land of

items.explanation: In Part II of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), Lemuel Gulliver voyages to the land of Brobdingnag, whose inhabitants are giant, mountain-like beings standing roughly sixty feet tall.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Patrick White
items.stem:
Patrick White's Voss is a novel
about

structured.lead: Patrick White's Voss is a novel about
structured.options_hint: the sea the capital market the landscape

items.explanation: Australian Nobel Laureate Patrick White's historical novel Voss (1957)—inspired by the nineteenth-century Prussian explorer Ludwig Leichhardt—centres on Johann Ulrich Voss's doomed expedition across the vast, unforgiving interior landscape of the Australian desert.

structured.options_hint: Welsh Scottish Irish Polish

items.explanation: Born in County Londonderry, Northern Ireland, Nobel Prize-winning poet Seamus Heaney (1939–2013) rooted his English-language poetry deeply in Irish rural life, history, bog landscapes, and political troubles.

To whom is Mary Shelley's famous work
Frankenstein dedicated ?
structured.options_hint: Lord Byron Claire Clairmont William Godw

items.explanation: Mary Shelley dedicated her 1818 Gothic novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus to her father, the radical political philosopher and novelist William Godwin, author of An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice and Caleb Williams.

structured.lead:

London by train ?
structured.options_hint: Aubade Church Going The Whitsun Wedding

items.explanation: Philip Larkin's title poem 'The Whitsun Weddings' (1964) records the speaker's observations during a Saturday afternoon train journey from Hull to London as noisy wedding parties see off newlywed couples at station after station.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Butler (Restoration, 1613–1680)
items.stem:

sharp edge of praise to attack his
victims was

structured.lead: The English satirist who used the sharp edge of praise to attack his victims was
structured.options_hint: Ben Jonson John Donne John Dryden Samuel

items.explanation: John Dryden perfected the mock-heroic technique of ironic, elevated praise to demolish his targets in satires like Mac Flecknoe and Absalom and Achitophel, comparing fine satire to 'the fineness of a stroke that separates the head from the body.'

items.explanation: The famous direct address 'Reader, I married him' opens the concluding chapter (Chapter 38) of Charlotte Brontë's Gothic bildungsroman Jane Eyre (1847), as Jane announces her marriage to the blinded Edward Rochester.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · William Langland

satire on

structured.lead: Langland's Piers Plowman is a satire on
structured.options_hint: aristocracy chivalry peasantry clergy

items.explanation: William Langland's fourteenth-century Middle English allegorical dream-vision poem Piers Plowman is a pointed religious and social satire directed primarily against the worldliness, greed, and moral corruption of the medieval clergy.

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

Shakespeare's

structured.lead:
Sexual jealousy is a theme in
Shakespeare's
structured.options_hint: The Merchant of Venice The Tempest Othel

items.explanation: Destructive sexual jealousy—famously described by Iago as 'the green-ey'd monster, which doth mock / The meat it feeds on'—is the central tragic theme of William Shakespeare's Othello (c. 1603–1604).

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Cleanth Brooks

structured.lead: The title, The New Criticism, published in 1941, was written by
structured.options_hint: Cleanth Brooks John Crowe Ransom Robert

items.explanation: American poet and critic John Crowe Ransom published his influential book The New Criticism in 1941, examining critics like I. A. Richards, T. S. Eliot, and Yvor Winters and giving the Anglo-American formalist movement its name.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · John Webster
items.stem:
Which of the following is not a
Revenge Tragedy ?

structured.lead:
Which of the following is not a
Revenge Tragedy ?
structured.options_hint: The White Devil The Duchess of Malfi Doc

items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (c. 1592) is a Renaissance tragedy of intellectual hubris and spiritual damnation modelled on the medieval morality play, whereas The Spanish Tragedy, The White Devil, and The Duchess of Malfi are revenge tragedies.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · John Galsworthy

structured.lead: Who of the following playwrights rejects the Aristotelian concept of tragic play as imitation of reality ?
structured.options_hint: Shaw Arthur Miller Bertolt Brecht John G

items.explanation: German modernist playwright Bertolt Brecht rejected Aristotelian dramatic mimesis, illusion, and emotional catharsis, developing instead 'non-Aristotelian' Epic Theatre and the Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) to provoke critical social reflection.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism

stressed syllable of two lines of
verse is called

structured.lead: A monosyllabic rhyme on the final stressed syllable of two lines of verse is called
structured.options_hint: monorhyme feminine rhyme masculine rhyme

items.explanation: In prosody, a masculine rhyme is a rhyme that falls on a single final stressed syllable at the ends of verse lines (such as 'still'/'hill' or 'comply'/'deny'), in contrast to a two-syllable feminine rhyme.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Salman Rushdie

Rushdie's name following the
publication of

structured.lead:
A fatwa was issued in Salman
Rushdie's name following the publication of
structured.options_hint: Midnight's Children Shame Satanic Verses

items.explanation: Following the 1988 publication of Salman Rushdie's fourth novel, The Satanic Verses, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa on 14 February 1989 calling for the author's death over alleged blasphemy.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
"There is nothing outside the text"
is a key statement emanating from

structured.lead: "There is nothing outside the text" is a key statement emanating from
structured.options_hint: Feminism New Historicism Deconstruction

items.explanation: 'There is nothing outside the text' ('Il n'y a pas de hors-texte') is Jacques Derrida's famous dictum from Of Grammatology (1967), a foundational statement of Deconstruction asserting that all meaning is mediated through linguistic signifiers and context.

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
The Augustan Age is called so
because

structured.lead: The Augustan Age is called so because
structured.options_hint: King Augustus ruled over England during

options: King Augustus ruled over England during this period
The English writers imitated the Roman writers during this period
The English King was born in the month of August
This was an age of sensibility
items.explanation: Early eighteenth-century English literature is called the Augustan Age because neoclassical writers like Pope, Swift, and Addison consciously admired and imitated the classical Roman poets—Virgil, Horace, and Ovid—who wrote under Emperor Augustus.

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Martin Amis

structured.options_hint: Time's Arrow by Martin Amis Portrait of

The French Lieutenant's Woman by John Fowles
items.explanation: Kingsley Amis's comic campus novel Lucky Jim (1954), along with John Osborne's play Look Back in Anger (1956), is a defining text of the 1950s British 'Angry Young Men' movement, expressing working- and lower-middle-class disillusionment with the establishment.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

items.explanation: In An Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735), Alexander Pope viciously satirizes the Whig courtier and memoirist John Hervey, 2nd Baron Hervey, under the portrait of 'Sporus,' mocking him as a 'painted child of dirt, that stinks and stings.'

items.explanation: In Christopher Marlowe's two-part play Tamburlaine the Great (c. 1587–1588), the central conqueror Tamburlaine begins life as a humble Scythian shepherd who casts off his 'shepherd's weeds' to become a mighty world emperor.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

structured.lead:
In a letter to his brother George in
September 1819, John Keats had this to say about a fellow romantic poet : "He describes what he sees -
I describe what I imagine - Mine is the hardest task." The poet under reference is
structured.options_hint: Wordsworth Coleridge Byron Southey

items.explanation: In his September 1819 journal-letter to George and Georgiana Keats, John Keats explicitly contrasts his own imaginative method with that of Lord Byron: 'You speak of Lord Byron and me – There is this great difference between us. He describes what he sees – I describe what I imagine.'

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

structured.options_hint: alliteration acrostic assent syllable

items.explanation: Alliteration is the stylistic device of repeating speech sounds—typically initial consonant sounds—in a sequence of nearby words within a line or phrase of verse or prose.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Reformation was predominantly a
movement in

structured.lead: Reformation was predominantly a movement in
structured.options_hint: politics literature religion education

items.explanation: The sixteenth-century Reformation, sparked by Martin Luther in 1517 and carried forward by John Calvin and the English Reformation, was predominantly a religious movement challenging Papal authority and Catholic doctrine to establish Protestantism.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · E. M. Forster
items.stem:
The motto "only connect" is taken
from

structured.lead: The motto "only connect" is taken from
structured.options_hint: Joseph Conrad's Nostromo Rudyard Kipling

options: Wells' The History of Mr. Polly
items.explanation: 'Only connect...' is the celebrated epigraph and central thematic leitmotif of E. M. Forster's novel Howards End (1910), advocating harmony between the pragmatic material world (the Wilcoxes) and the inner life of culture and emotion (the Schlegels).

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
English Iambic Pentameter was
brought to its first maturity in

structured.lead: English Iambic Pentameter was brought to its first maturity in
structured.options_hint: sonnet dramatic verse lyric elegy

items.explanation: Although introduced into English verse Earlier, iambic pentameter was brought to its first full expressive maturity and flexibility in Elizabethan dramatic verse (blank verse), perfected on the stage by Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

Who among the following was not

structured.options_hint: Lytton Strachey Clive Bell Forster Winst

items.explanation: Biographer Lytton Strachey, art critic Clive Bell, and novelist E. M. Forster were core members of the early twentieth-century Bloomsbury Group alongside Virginia Woolf and John Maynard Keynes, whereas Prime Minister Winston Churchill was never part of the circle.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
The concept of human mind as
tabula rasa or blank tablet was
propounded by

structured.lead: The concept of human mind as tabula rasa or blank tablet was propounded by
structured.options_hint: Bishop Berkley David Hume Francis Bacon

items.explanation: English empiricist philosopher John Locke propounded the concept of the human mind at birth as a tabula rasa ('blank slate' or 'white paper,' void of innate ideas and inscribed solely through sensory experience) in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689).

items.explanation: New Historicist critic Stephen Greenblatt introduced andpaired the concepts of 'resonance' (the historical and cultural network surrounding an object) and 'wonder' (the arresting aesthetic power of the object itself) in his 1990 essay 'Resonance and Wonder.'

items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer composed the General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales in decasyllabic (ten-syllabic) rhyming couplets (iambic pentameter), moving away from his earlier French-influenced octosyllabic verse.

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Charles Darwin

structured.lead: Charles Darwin's Origin of the Species was published in the year

items.explanation: Charles Darwin's groundbreaking evolutionary treatise On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection was published on 24 November 1859, profoundly unsettling Victorian religious faith and literary thought.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

structured.options_hint: Lady Gregory Yeats Oscar Wilde Sean O'Ca

items.explanation: Juno and the Paycock (1924) is a celebrated tragicomedy by Irish playwright Sean O'Casey. Set in the Dublin tenements during the Irish Civil War, it forms the middle play of O'Casey's Dublin Trilogy.

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Faulkner

The title of William Faulkner's The
Sound and the Fury is taken from a play by
structured.options_hint: Christopher Marlowe William Shakespeare

items.explanation: William Faulkner took the title of his 1929 modernist novel The Sound and the Fury from Macbeth's famous soliloquy in Act V, Scene v of William Shakespeare's tragedy Macbeth: 'it is a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.'

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

"Silverman has never read
Browning." This is an example of
structured.options_hint: chiasmus conceit zeugma metonymy

items.explanation: The sentence 'Silverman has never read Browning' is an example of metonymy, a figure of speech in which a closely associated name—here the author 'Browning'—is substituted for the thing meant, namely the poems written by Robert Browning.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2010 (Paper II)

structured.lead: Which Eliotian character utters the question - "Do I eat a peach" ?
structured.options_hint: Marina Prufrock Sweeney Stetson

items.explanation: The anxious, aging speaker J. Alfred Prufrock utters the famous self-doubting question 'Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach?' near the close of T. S. Eliot's dramatic monologue 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (1915).

structured.lead: Which among the following works by Daniel Defoe landed him in prison and the pillory ?
structured.options_hint: The True-Born Englishman Captain Singlet

items.explanation: Daniel Defoe's anonymous 1702 pamphlet The Shortest Way with the Dissenters—an ironic satire impersonating an extreme High Church Tory demanding the extermination of Nonconformists—led to his arrest, imprisonment in Newgate, and three days in the pillory in 1703.

structured.options_hint: Sir Thomas Malory John Gower John Barbou

items.explanation: English merchant, diplomat, and translator William Caxton introduced the printing press to England at Westminster in 1476, printing landmark Middle English works including Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales and Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur.

structured.lead:
About which nineteenth century
English writer was it said that "He had succeeded as a writer not by conforming to the Spirit of the Age, but in opposition to it" ?
structured.options_hint: Lord Byron on Coleridge Coleridge on Kea

items.explanation: In his collection of critical portraits The Spirit of the Age (1825), William Hazlitt wrote of his friend and fellow essayist Charles Lamb ('Elia'): 'Mr. Lamb has succeeded, not by conforming to the Spirit of the Age, but in opposition to it.'
